Today, we’re excited to announce the general availability of our next-generation Storage-optimized Z4M machine series in Google Compute Engine, available as both Virtual Machine (VM) and bare-metal instances.

We built Z4M to provide storage for AI/ML training and inference workloads such as checkpointing, distributed key-value (KV) cache and parallel file systems — workloads that handle huge data volumes and require massive parallel data processing, as well as high storage and networking throughput. Low latency access to data is equally critical to keep GPUs and TPUs fully utilized. Powered by the fifth-generation Intel Xeon Scalable processors and paired with the latest enhancements in Titanium, Z4M provides up to 168,000 GiB of Local SSD (LSSD) storage coupled with up to 400 Gbps of Cloud Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) networking. RDMA improves the performance of these demanding workloads by reducing data-access latency by up to 60% compared to TCP networking, so you can increase your applications’ throughput while right-sizing your cloud investment.

The Z4M VM portfolio lets you scale your infrastructure and clusters to meet workload requirements by providing a large total LSSD capacity as well as 875 GiB of LSSD capacity per vCPU. Further, Z4M bare-metal instances give you direct access to the physical hardware without a virtualization layer, reducing latency for workloads such as custom hypervisors and workloads with specific licensing needs. items.excerpt:
In July 2026, U.S. imports of crude oil from Venezuela averaged 701,000 barrels per day (b/d), the most since May 2017, before decreasing to 655,000 b/d in August, according to data published in our Petroleum Supply Monthly.

Crude oil imports from Venezuela started the year at 200,000 b/d and have steadily increased most months this year. Increased imports from Venezuela are supported by high crude oil demand from U.S. refineries because of high global refinery margins and the easing of U.S. government restrictions on purchases from the country. Many refineries on the U.S. Gulf Coast (PADD 3) are configured to process heavy sour crude oil grades, such as those from Venezuela.

According to data from Vortexa, the majority of crude oil exports from Venezuela in 2025 were destined for China. In 2026, Venezuela has exported no crude oil to China, and the United States has instead been the largest single destination by volume for Venezuelan crude oil exports.

U.S. crude oil imports from Venezuela stopped shortly after the United States imposed sanctions on state oil company Petróleos de Venezuela SA (PDVSA) in January 2019. In November 2022, the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control granted Chevron waivers to resume exporting crude oil from its joint venture operations in Venezuela to U.S. Gulf Coast refineries; Chevron resumed these exports in January 2023.

items.excerpt:
AI agents do more than generate answers. They search for information, query databases, write and test code and take action.

Each of those steps relies on a CPU, with agents moving between GPU reasoning and CPU execution throughout a task.

As businesses put more agents to work, AI factories need CPUs that can execute those steps quickly and support many agents at once, all within the limits of available power.

What this means: AI infrastructure providers need to support more agents without making each one wait longer to get work done. And critically, AI factories are power limited. This means operators need to choose infrastructure that maximizes the work done for every watt.

Why it matters: NVIDIA Vera delivers both fast agent performance and high capacity per watt within a single CPU. That gives providers one CPU for a range of agent workloads, rather than having to mix and match fast and dense x86 parts to balance speed and capacity.

The data that proves it: In a 100-megawatt data center comparison, NVIDIA found that a single Vera CPU performs better than the fastest x86 CPU and the most energy-efficient x86 CPU.

Every day, more and more people are using coding agents like Google Antigravity and OpenCode to complete software engineering tasks. But those tools need instructions to operate and their output is only as good as the inputs they get. By utilizing agent skills that direct the agents through building, testing, and deploying code, developers have a powerful way to automate their workflows.

But most skills are written manually, so it’s hard to know which instructions are effective without assessing their output.

To measure the effectiveness of our skills, we ran OpenCode with Gemini 3.8 Flash on tasks from Terminal-Bench 2.0, a public benchmark. The results were inconclusive: with our baseline skill, the agent passed about two-thirds of its attempts, but the outcome was about the same even without the skill. We needed better results.

To achieve them, we turned to AlphaEvolve, which optimizes skills the way it optimizes code: Gemini proposes a new version, an evaluator scores it, and the search retains the higher-scoring version. For more than a decade, BigQuery has helped set standards for structured data aggregation, calculating financial sums, counting active users, and computing historical averages at a petabyte scale in seconds. Larger models, longer contexts and agentic applications are increasing GPU memory pressure while supply tightens and prices rise — a trend expected to continue through the near term.

NVIDIA works closely with memory partners to rapidly adopt the latest memory technologies. NVIDIA was first to adopt HBM3e and HBM4 technologies into an accelerated computing stack.

But the approach isn’t to simply pack more memory onto the GPU. It’s full-stack codesign. NVIDIA intentionally designs GPUs, CPUs, networking, storage and software together to get more useful work out of memory at every layer of the AI factory.

That matters because an AI factory runs on a memory and storage hierarchy. GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is the fastest, most expensive and most contested tier — with model weights and KV cache competing for limited capacity. Below it sit CPU memory, local SSDs and shared storage, each trading speed for more capacity at a lower cost per bit.

How much useful work a byte does depends on how well the whole hierarchy is used: shrinking what must be stored, placing it on the right tier and bringing it back to the GPU before it’s needed.

Petroleum refinery yields represent the share of a specific fuel that is produced from each barrel of crude oil a given refinery (or group of refineries) processes. The U.S. refining fleet tends to have a strong refinery yield of gasoline—typically between 45%–50%. In general terms, for every 100 barrels of crude oil U.S. refiners process, they produce about 45–50 barrels of gasoline. Typically, the most important refinery yields in the United States are the refinery yields of motor gasoline, distillate fuel oil (often sold as diesel fuel), and kerosene-type jet fuel. The combined yield of motor gasoline, distillate fuel oil, and jet fuel typically accounts for between 85%–90% of the petroleum products produced by the U.S. refining fleet.

Ready to modernize your infrastructure without risking production stability? API multi-versioning for Compute Engine, now in general availability, helps you do just that. With date-based API versions, Compute Engine can now regularly deliver modern API semantics, stronger resilience defaults, and improved developer experience while preserving the rock-solid stability of the /v1 API.

For more than a decade, the Google Compute Engine /v1 API has served as the foundational control plane for millions of virtual machines, Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) clusters, and large-scale AI infrastructure. For platform teams and developers who build on Google Cloud, that single /v1 endpoint delivered an extraordinary promise: write your integration once, and trust that it will keep running year after year.

Yet as cloud architectures have grown in scale and sophistication, infrastructure teams have faced a growing tension. In addition, we’re announcing the general availability of AlloyDB sync and Lakehouse federation. Together, they give AlloyDB three ways to work with the borderless Lakehouse, which keeps one open copy of your data available to any engine. Etsy, for example, unified three petabytes with the borderless Lakehouse, joining data in place to accelerate pipeline queries by 60%. With AlloyDB, which approach to use depends on where the data lives and how your application reads it:

Direct Iceberg access: Read Iceberg tables in place, accelerated by the AlloyDB columnar engine.

AlloyDB sync: Serve lakehouse data from AlloyDB for your most latency-sensitive workloads, refreshed on a schedule you set.

Lakehouse federation: Query native BigQuery tables in place, with BigQuery doing the processing.

items.excerpt:
Clinical Evaluation Lead, Google for Health

Many of us have turned to AI with a health question or received care from a doctor who’s using it. The adoption of technology for health is accelerating and impacts billions of people every day. But how can we assess if these tools are safe and helpful?

In partnership with health experts Dr. Elizabeth McGlynn and Dr. Dana Gelb Safran, we published a whitepaper detailing an end-to-end evaluation approach to assess AI use cases for addressing people’s health needs. The framework evaluates models across three areas: accuracy, safety, and usefulness. It combines closed-question benchmarks, autoraters, and expert human review to assess common and high-risk health scenarios.

We built and continue to utilize this framework to assess whether our models provide useful, accurate responses that promote safe interactions in health contexts. By sharing our methodology, we hope to promote transparency in how we approach this important area, and seek to support the entire health ecosystem — from developers to researchers to clinicians — in building AI tools people can trust.

Over the past few years, our Google Cloud Consulting team has partnered with many companies to introduce AI into their daily operations.

In that time, we’ve seen the focus shift from generative AI that answers questions to agentic systems that fully carry out the work. These agents can create multi-step plans and manage a project from start to finish.

While budget, compute, and tooling can help launch an agent program, enterprise adoption takes intentional culture work. People need to feel empowered enough to experiment with agents, and leaders need to show teams what agents mean for their roles.

Based on our work across these organizations, we’ve put together five practical lessons for guiding enterprises through an agentic shift.

Most enterprise workflows run like a relay race: one person completes a task, checks it, and hands it off to the next person, who then does the same. Layering an AI agent onto that model gives you a faster runner for one leg, but the handoffs may stall or slow down other work.

Redesigning your workflows can remove blockers like these in a few ways:

Strategic direction: Move from human-in-the-loop validation (where a person checks each step) to a human-in-the-lead model. Agents take on the work, and people set the direction and own the outcomes.
